Despite advancements in early detection and adjuvant treatments, such as chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, and targeted therapies, metastatic breast cancer still carries a poor prognosis, with a five-year survival rate of less than 30% [ 1 ]. The latest data from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) through the GLOBOCAN 2018 report, which encompasses information from 185 countries, revealed that breast cancer is responsible for 2.3 million new cases annually, representing 11.7% of all cancers, and a mortality rate of 6.9% [ 2 ]. The growing global burden of breast cancer presents an urgent need for effective strategies to mitigate the incidence, mortality, and associated morbidity of the disease, making it a significant concern for many countries. Breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease with complex risk factors and diverse etiologies [ 3 – 5 ]. Its clinical manifestations, treatment responses, and prognoses are influenced by various genetic, lifestyle, environmental, and demographic factors [ 6 , 7 ]. Despite its global prevalence, there are marked regional disparities in breast cancer incidence, mortality, and survival outcomes. These differences are attributed to a combination of factors such as healthcare infrastructure, access to treatment, and socio-economic conditions. For instance, in developed countries, lifestyle factors such as late-night work schedules, delayed childbirth, hormonal replacement therapy, and shifts in reproductive patterns, such as later age at marriage and first childbearing, are known to contribute significantly to breast cancer risk [ 8 , 9 ]. On the other hand, in low and middle-income countries, the primary barriers to reducing breast cancer mortality include insufficient medical facilities, delayed diagnosis, inadequate or non-existent screening programs, and limited public awareness about the disease [ 10 , 11 ]. Advances in breast cancer treatment have significantly improved the survival rates of patients, with therapies ranging from surgery and chemotherapy to immunotherapy, radiation, and emerging targeted treatments [ 10 , 12 , 13 ]. The increasing number of women surviving breast cancer diagnoses [ 2 ] further emphasizes the importance of identifying the lifestyle and risk factors that contribute to mortality, in order to enhance treatment outcomes and inform preventative strategies. Despite a large body of research investigating breast cancer risk factors, much of the existing literature has focused on specific geographic locations, case studies, or limited populations, resulting in a fragmented understanding of the broader global trends in breast cancer mortality. While these studies have contributed valuable insights into particular risk factors, they often do not provide a comprehensive analysis of the global factors influencing breast cancer-related deaths. Furthermore, there remains a scarcity of research that systematically consolidates and synthesizes data on common causes of breast cancer mortality across diverse populations and regions. Despite growing global interest in breast cancer outcomes, most existing meta-analyses have focused narrowly on specific biomarkers, treatment effects, or high-income country populations, often overlooking the broader interplay between clinical, demographic, and socio-environmental determinants of mortality. This study offers a distinct advancement by integrating evidence from a large and diverse set of studies spanning multiple regions—including low- and middle-income countries that are frequently underrepresented in the literature. By synthesizing findings across varied healthcare contexts, this meta-analysis captures a more globally representative picture of mortality risk in breast cancer patients. Moreover, it highlights the prognostic impact of non-traditional factors such as comorbidity profiles, geographic disparities, and social determinants like education and access to care. In doing so, this work moves beyond previous reviews that often treated these dimensions in isolation, offering instead a comprehensive, comparative analysis that supports more equitable and context-sensitive strategies for improving breast cancer survival outcomes worldwide. Materials and methods Study protocol This meta-analysis aims to systematically review high-quality research that assesses the impact of various risk factors on breast cancer mortality. To ensure a rigorous and transparent methodology, we adhered to the guidelines set forth by the “Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses” (PRISMA) framework [ 14 ]. The systematic review involved a comprehensive search of relevant studies from multiple databases, including peer-reviewed articles, cohort studies, case-control studies, and randomized controlled trials, that specifically investigate the association between different risk factors and breast cancer mortality. Search strategies A comprehensive literature search was conducted up to June 2025 across the following electronic databases: MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, and Open Research Dataset. The search strategy was developed in collaboration with a medical librarian with expertise in systematic review methodology, to ensure the rigor and completeness of the search process. For the MEDLINE database, we used Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) in combination with keywords such as “Breast cancer,” “mortality,” “death,” and “survival.” In other databases that do not support MeSH (e.g., Scopus, EMBASE), equivalent keywords and database-specific indexing terms were applied. The complete search strategies for all databases, including exact strings, Boolean logic, and database-specific syntax, are provided in Supplement 25 to ensure transparency and reproducibility. The search was tailored to identify studies reporting clinical status, laboratory findings, and sociodemographic characteristics associated with mortality in breast cancer patients. All search results were imported into EndNote X9 for citation management and screening. Eligibility criteria After removing duplicates, the remaining records were screened by title and abstract to identify potentially relevant studies, followed by full-text assessment based on predefined eligibility criteria (Fig. 1 ). Studies were excluded if they lacked full-text access, were non-original (e.g., reviews, editorials, theses, or letters), or did not report relevant statistical data. Fig. 1 Flow chart of search strategy and selection criteria To ensure consistency and validity, only studies reporting adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) or adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals were included. Unadjusted estimates were excluded unless corresponding adjusted values were available through supplementary data or author correspondence. When multiple models were reported, we selected the model adjusted for the greatest number of relevant covariates. Additionally, only studies reporting breast cancer–specific survival as the outcome were included, ensuring the analysis focused on mortality directly attributable to breast cancer. Assessment for study quality and data extraction The appropriateness of the search outputs for inclusion in the meta-analysis was assessed independently by each author to ensure that only relevant studies were selected. Any discrepancies or differences in opinion regarding inclusion were resolved through discussion and mutual agreement. A wide range of data was extracted from each selected study, including sample size, outcome (mortality), publication year, author names, countries, and study design. The clinical variables examined included histological grade, lymph node status, stage of the disease, comorbidities, and treatment modalities such as lumpectomy with radiation, chemotherapy, trastuzumab, hormonal therapy, surgical therapy, and chemotherapy, as well as tumor size. Demographic variables such as age, BMI, smoking status, race, postmenopausal status, and educational level were also considered as potential factors influencing breast cancer mortality. Furthermore, hazard ratios (HR) and odds ratios (OR), along with their respective 95% confidence intervals (CI), were extracted to quantify the relationship between these variables and breast cancer mortality. The authors employed the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale [ 15 ] to independently evaluate the methodological quality of the included studies. This scale evaluates three main components: comparability of study groups, evaluation of the results, and patient selection. Each of the seven domains in the Newcastle-Ottawa approach was scored on a scale from 0 to 3 (ranging from low to high bias), and an average score was calculated to assess the overall study quality. The overall quality assessment tool, along with the associated point values, is detailed in Supplement 24. This rigorous assessment ensured that only studies of sufficient methodological quality were included in the meta-analysis, providing a robust analysis of the relationship between various risk factors and breast cancer mortality. Statistical analysis The main outcome of interest was the difference in mortality. We used HRs or ORs (with 95%CI) from peer-reviewed published studies to examine the relationship between breast cancer mortality and risk factors. Using the random-effects model, the overall effect size for breast cancer mortality in relation to risk factors was determined. When employing a random-effects model, the expected between-study heterogeneity has been taken into account. To assess heterogeneity, we computed the Cochran Q test and I 2 statistic. The presence of heterogeneity in effect sizes was assessed using Cochran’s Q test; a significant Q value indicates the presence of heterogeneity as opposed to homogeneity. The percentage of the total variance that may be attributed to study heterogeneity was determined using the I 2 statistic [ 16 ]. Accordingly, mild, moderate, and severe heterogeneity classifications were given to I 2 levels falling between 0% and 39%, 40% and 59%, and 60% and 90%, respectively [ 16 ]. The Egger weighted regression test was used to assess publication bias [ 17 ]. For each analysis, STATA version 18 and R-4.1.1 statistical tools were used to calculate the pooled effect sizes and publication biases. All p-values reported were tested at α = 0.05 level. Results Search results A total of 181 records were identified through database searching, including MEDLINE ( n = 10), EMBASE ( n = 7), Scopus ( n = 61), Cochrane Library ( n = 8), Web of Science ( n = 28), and Google Scholar ( n = 71). After removing 25 duplicate records, 160 records remained for screening, of which 25 were excluded based on title and abstract review. Full texts were sought for 135 articles; however, 15 could not be retrieved. The remaining 120 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 52 were excluded for reasons including poor quality ( n = 4), qualitative study design ( n = 7), non-English language ( n = 8), review articles ( n = 14), and failure to report adjusted hazard or odds ratios (aHR/aOR) ( n = 19). Ultimately, 70 studies met all inclusion criteria and were included in the final systematic review and meta-analysis. The detailed selection process is illustrated in Fig. 1 . All 70 included studies accounted for a broad range of demographic, clinical, and treatment-related variables. These included age, body mass index (BMI), estrogen/progesterone receptor (ER/PR) status, tumor size, race, physical activity, treatment type (e.g., chemotherapy with trastuzumab, hormonal therapy), histological grade, lymph node status, disease stage, education level, smoking status, and other relevant covariates. Study quality was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for observational studies, which assesses three domains: selection (maximum 4 points), comparability (maximum 2 points), and outcome/exposure (maximum 3 points). Individual domain-level scores for all included studies are presented in Supplement 24. Overall, the studies demonstrated strong methodological quality, with NOS scores ranging from 7 to 9, indicating a low risk of bias (see Supplement 24). Geographical distribution and demographic characteristics A detailed summary of all the selected studies [ 5 , 18 – 56 ] can be found in Supplement 23. The majority of these studies were published between 2020 and 2025, reflecting recent research on breast cancer mortality. Geographically, twelve studies were conducted in the United States, ten in China, eight in Ethiopia, four in South Africa, three each in Brazil, Canada, and Kenya, and two in Malaysia. The remaining studies were carried out in various European countries and other regions worldwide. In total, these studies reported data from 2,447,155 patients, with individual sample sizes ranging from 79 to 1,192,294 patients (Supplement 23 and Fig. 2 ). This wide-ranging dataset provides a robust basis for assessing the impact of various risk factors on breast cancer mortality across different populations and settings. Fig. 2 Forest plot showing the mortality rate of breast cancer Pooled mortality rate of breast cancer Figure 2 displays the results from the random-effects model, which highlighted the considerable variation in breast cancer mortality rates across the included studies. The death rates ranged from as low as 0.70% (95% CI: 0.61-0.81%) [ 18 ] to as high as 72.35% (95% CI: 68.44-76.03%) [ 30 ]. Overall, the studies included data from 2,447,155 patients, with a total of 160,284 reported deaths, resulting in a pooled mortality rate of 16.89% (95% CI: 12.94-21.76%). Further analysis of hot spot analysis results in breast cancer mortality revealed that the highest mortality rates were observed in Africa, while North America exhibited the lowest rates, highlighting distinct regional differences in outcomes (see Fig. 3 ). This variation underscores the importance of considering socio-demographic, healthcare, and environmental factors when analyzing breast cancer mortality on a global scale. Fig. 3 Regional distribution of pooled breast cancer mortality prevalence worldwide Predictors of breast cancer mortality The meta-analysis examined several risk factors associated with breast cancer mortality across multiple studies. The analysis revealed that being classified as Luminal B compared to Luminal A was associated with a significantly higher risk of mortality, with an effect size of 1.93 (95% CI: 1.19–2.68) based on five studies (See Table 1 and Supplement 1). Lumpectomy with radiation was found to significantly reduce mortality, with an effect size of 0.66 (95% CI: 0.55–0.77) across three studies. Chemotherapy combined with trastuzumab also demonstrated a reduction in mortality, yielding an effect size of 0.60 (95% CI: 0.47–0.73), based on three studies. High allostatic load was identified as a risk factor for increased mortality, with an effect size of 1.26 (95% CI: 1.02–1.49). Additionally, having an advanced ECOG performance status (PS) was associated with an increased risk of mortality, with an effect size of 1.54 (95% CI: 1.28–1.82), based on the same number of studies (See Table 1 and Supplement 1–5). Treatments such as hormonal therapy (effect size = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.63–0.90) and surgical therapy (effect size = 0.57, 95% CI: 0.46–0.68) showed a protective effect, lowering the risk of mortality. Chemotherapy was also associated with reduced mortality risk, with an effect size of 0.63 (95% CI: 0.51–0.74). Additionally, positive estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) status were linked to a decrease in mortality risk, with effect sizes of 0.59 (95% CI: 0.53–0.65) and 0.66 (95% CI: 0.57–0.75), respectively. (See Table 1 and Supplement 6–10). On the other hand, factors like HIV positivity and lymph node involvement increased the risk of breast cancer mortality. HIV-positive patients had an elevated mortality risk (effect size = 1.45, 95% CI: 1.22–1.69), while patients with positive lymph nodes had a much higher risk (effect size = 2.24, 95% CI: 1.71–2.77). Furthermore, diabetes was associated with an increased risk of mortality (effect size = 1.21, 95% CI: 1.05–1.37). (See Table 1 and Supplement 10–13). A large tumor size was associated with an increased risk of mortality (effect size = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.46–2.06), while advanced tumor grade and stage also showed strong associations with higher mortality risks, with effect sizes of 1.85 (95% CI: 1.50–2.20) and 2.76 (95% CI: 2.25–3.27), respectively. These results highlight the importance of tumor characteristics in predicting patient outcomes. (See Table 1 and Supplement 14–16). Obesity was also found to be a significant risk factor for breast cancer mortality, with an effect size of 1.33 (95% CI: 1.08–1.59), indicating that individuals with obesity have a higher likelihood of poorer outcomes. These findings underscore the critical role of both disease progression markers, such as tumor size, grade, and stage, as well as lifestyle factors like obesity, in influencing breast cancer survival rates. (See Table 1 and Supplement 18). The meta-analysis also identified several demographic and lifestyle factors influencing breast cancer mortality. Black race was found to be a significant risk factor, with an effect size of 1.45 (95% CI: 1.22–1.68), indicating a higher likelihood of mortality among Black women. Older age also correlated with increased mortality, with an effect size of 1.66 (95% CI: 1.35–1.97), highlighting that age is an important determinant of breast cancer survival outcomes. In contrast, higher educational level appeared to be associated with a reduced risk of mortality, with an effect size of 0.58 (95% CI: 0.37–0.78), suggesting that women with higher education may have better outcomes, possibly due to access to healthcare and health literacy. Additionally, current smoking was associated with a significantly higher mortality risk, with an effect size of 1.92 (95% CI: 1.01–2.83), emphasizing the detrimental impact of smoking on breast cancer survival. These results suggest that both socio-demographic factors and lifestyle behaviors play a significant role in shaping breast cancer mortality risks. Meta-regression analysis To explore sources of heterogeneity, we conducted meta-regression analyses using study-level variables including region, sample size, and publication year. The analysis identified geographic region and sample size as significant moderators for several risk factors. For example, larger studies showed significantly lower heterogeneity for the effects of covariates on mortality ( p = 0.01), while studies from LMICs reported more pronounced effects for HIV status and late-stage diagnosis. Full results are provided in Supplementary 26. Heterogeneity, sensitivity, and publication bias The heterogeneity and publication bias analysis of the meta-analysis revealed significant variation across several risk factors. For example, lumpectomy with radiation (I² = 85.77%, p = 0.000) and large tumor size (I² = 87.12%, p = 0.000) exhibited high heterogeneity, suggesting substantial differences in the effect sizes among the studies. Other factors, such as advanced ECOG performance status (I² = 0.00%, p = 0.490), showed no heterogeneity, indicating consistent findings across studies. Significant heterogeneity was also observed in risk factors like luminal B (I² = 64.55%, p = 0.013), high allostatic load (I² = 80.46%, p = 0.000), and chemotherapy (I² = 96.13%, p = 0.000), while factors like hormonal therapy (I² = 32.07%, p = 0.310) and surgical therapy (I² = 31.40%, p = 0.260) showed relatively lower or non-significant heterogeneity. Regarding publication bias, Egger’s test showed no significant evidence of bias for all risk factors (see Table 1 ). Discussion The present meta-analysis aimed to identify and quantify key risk factors associated with breast cancer mortality by synthesizing data across a wide range of studies. Our findings confirm the multifactorial nature of breast cancer prognosis, highlighting the interplay of clinical characteristics, sociodemographic variables, and lifestyle-related factors. Importantly, meta-regression analyses revealed that geographic region and sample size significantly contributed to the observed heterogeneity in effect estimates. Studies conducted in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) tended to report stronger associations for certain risk factors—while smaller sample sizes were linked to greater variability in mortality outcomes. These results emphasize the importance of contextual factors in shaping survival patterns and the need to interpret pooled estimates within the framework of study-level characteristics. In terms of scope, this review represents one of the most comprehensive meta-analyses to date on breast cancer mortality, covering diverse exposures including therapeutic interventions, comorbid conditions, and social determinants of health. Our findings indicate a pooled mortality rate of 16.89%, which aligns with results from previous studies examining breast cancer mortality rates across various populations [ 2 ]. Additionally, the regional differences revealed in our hot spot analysis, showing the highest mortality rates in Africa and the lowest in North America, are consistent with prior research highlighting these disparities [ 57 , 58 ]. This geographical variation underscores the significance of regional healthcare interventions and emphasizes the need for targeted public health strategies to address the global disparities in breast cancer mortality. Our meta-analysis found that being classified as Luminal B compared to Luminal A was significantly associated with a higher risk of mortality. This finding is consistent with previous studies that have reported Luminal B subtype as a more aggressive form of breast cancer, associated with poorer survival outcomes compared to Luminal A. For instance, a study by Li et al. [ 59 ] highlighted that Luminal B breast cancer is often characterized by higher proliferative activity and a higher risk of recurrence, leading to worse overall survival. Similarly, studies by Lammers et al. [ 60 ] also reported that Luminal B breast cancer has worse prognosis compared to Luminal A, likely due to its higher grade and hormonal therapy resistance. These findings underscore the importance of subtype classification in predicting mortality and guiding treatment decisions for breast cancer patients. High allostatic load as a significant risk factor for increased mortality in breast cancer patients in our analysis. This finding aligns with recent research that underscores the impact of chronic stress and physiological wear-and-tear, as measured by allostatic load, on cancer prognosis. A study by Obeng-Gyasi et al. [ 61 ] found that high allostatic load, reflecting the cumulative burden of chronic stress, was associated with poorer survival outcomes in breast cancer patients. Additionally, a study by Mathew et al. [ 62 ] confirmed that elevated allostatic load, including markers such as cortisol levels and inflammatory cytokines, correlated with worse outcomes in cancer survival, further supporting our results. Furthermore, research by Yang et al. [ 63 ] highlighted that individuals with higher allostatic load had a significantly increased risk of mortality across various diseases, including cancer, demonstrating that the physiological consequences of prolonged stress can adversely affect cancer prognosis. These findings suggest that incorporating allostatic load measurements in clinical assessments may help identify breast cancer patients at higher risk, emphasizing the importance of stress management and psychosocial interventions in cancer care. Our meta-analysis revealed that lumpectomy with radiation significantly reduced mortality. This finding is consistent with previous studies, which have demonstrated that breast-conserving surgery followed by radiation is an effective treatment strategy for reducing mortality in early-stage breast cancer patients. For instance, A study by found that combination of lumpectomy and radiation significantly reduced recurrence rates and mortality. Similarly, a study by found that patients who underwent a lumpectomy followed by radiation therapy generally have longer survival rates compared to those who only had a lumpectomy These findings confirm the continued relevance of lumpectomy with radiation as an optimal treatment option for early breast cancer. Chemotherapy combined with trastuzumab was found to reduce mortality in our analysis. This result is consistent with more recent studies and meta-analyses that continue to underscore the efficacy of this combination in improving survival outcomes for patients with breast cancer. A landmark study, the CLEOPATRA trial, demonstrated that adding trastuzumab to chemotherapy resulted in a significant improvement in progression-free survival and overall survival for patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer [ 64 ]. Similarly, the APHINITY trial, a large-scale study, found that the addition of pertuzumab and trastuzumab to chemotherapy reduced the risk of recurrence and improved survival in early-stage HER2-positive breast cancer [ 65 ]. Furthermore, a meta-analysis by Bradley et al. [ 66 ] reaffirmed the survival benefit of trastuzumab in combination with chemotherapy in breast cancer patients, supporting our findings of reduced mortality. These findings reinforce the clinical importance of trastuzumab in improving breast cancer outcomes. Our meta-analysis revealed that HIV-positive patients had an elevated risk of breast cancer mortality, which is consistent with recent studies highlighting the adverse impact of HIV on cancer outcomes. A study by Hernández-Ramírez et al. [ 67 ] demonstrated that HIV-infected individuals have an increased risk of various cancers, including breast cancer, due to immunosuppression and the effects of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Similarly, a more recent study by Ferreira et al. [ 68 ] found that breast cancer patients living with HIV experience worse survival outcomes compared to their HIV-negative counterparts, which they attributed to factors such as immune dysfunction and delayed diagnosis. In line with our findings, research also reported that HIV infection contributes to an increased risk of mortality in breast cancer patients, possibly due to complications like comorbidities and the immunological consequences of HIV [ 69 ]. These studies reinforce the need for tailored interventions for HIV-positive breast cancer patients, addressing both cancer-specific and HIV-related health challenges to improve survival outcomes. Diabetes was determined to be a substantial risk factor for breast cancer mortality based on our systematic study. Previous research also found that diabetic breast cancer patients had poorer survival rates compared to non-diabetic patients, which they attributed to factors such as insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and potential treatment delays [ 70 , 71 ]. Similarly, a study by Shao et al. [ 45 ] reported that diabetes was significantly associated with an increased risk of breast cancer-related mortality, suggesting that metabolic dysregulation and comorbid conditions in diabetic patients could contribute to worse outcomes. In line with our findings, research by Lega et al. [ 72 ] also confirmed that diabetes negatively impacts the prognosis of breast cancer patients, emphasizing the importance of addressing diabetes management in this patient population to improve survival. These findings underscore the need for better clinical management of diabetes in breast cancer patients to mitigate the associated risks. Obesity was determined to be a substantial risk factor for breast cancer mortality based on our systematic study. This finding is consistent with several previous studies. A comprehensive review by Rose et al. [ 73 ] demonstrated that obesity, particularly in postmenopausal women, is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer mortality due to mechanisms such as inflammation, insulin resistance, and hormonal imbalances. Additionally, a meta-analysis by Lohmann et al. [ 74 ] also confirmed that Obesity was associated with worse disease free breast cancer survival. Similarly, work by Pati et al. [ 75 ] suggested that obesity may exacerbate treatment-related side effects and influence decisions regarding specific cancer therapies. These findings collectively reinforce the need for targeted interventions addressing obesity in breast cancer patients to improve survival rates and reduce associated risks. Our meta-analysis confirmed that smoking significantly increases the risk of mortality from breast cancer, a finding that aligns with recent literature. A study by Goldvaser et al. [ 76 ] reported that smoking is a critical modifiable risk factor for breast cancer survival, particularly for women with estrogen receptor-negative tumors, who face worse prognosis. In a similar vein, a study by Lai et al. [ 32 ] found that women who had ever smoked had a significantly higher risk of breast cancer mortality compared to never-smokers, with the highest risks seen in current smokers. Furthermore, a work by Jiang et al. [ 77 ] demonstrated that smoking increases the likelihood of adverse treatment outcomes and poor prognosis, as smoking-related systemic inflammation and reduced immune function contribute to worse survival outcomes. These findings underline the critical need for smoking cessation interventions as part of cancer care to improve survival rates and reduce the long-term risks associated with breast cancer. Our meta-analysis confirms that breast cancer mortality is higher among Black women, which is consistent with a growing body of recent research highlighting racial disparities in breast cancer outcomes. A study by Hoskins et al. [ 78 ] found that Black women are more likely to be diagnosed with aggressive subtypes of breast cancer, such as triple-negative breast cancer, which contributes to their higher mortality rates. Similarly, a study by Miller-Kleinhenz et al. [ 79 ] highlighted that Black women experience later-stage diagnoses, less favorable tumor biology, and delayed access to healthcare, all of which exacerbate their risk of poor outcomes. Additionally, a study by Hunt et al. [ 80 ] identified socio-economic disparities, such as lower income and insurance status, as key factors driving these higher mortality rates among Black women. These findings reinforce the need for targeted interventions to address racial disparities in breast cancer diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes, including increased access to early screening, personalized treatments, and healthcare services for Black women. We also found that a higher breast cancer death rate is linked to an older diagnosis age. This outcome is in line with the research findings carried out by [ 81 , 82 ]. A plausible reason for this might be breast cancer in older patients might display more aggressive tumor biology and thereby increase mortality from breast cancer [ 83 ]. Our systematic review results also confirmed that higher education levels were significantly associated with lower mortality rates. This result was similar to the findings of previous studies [ 84 , 85 ], where a positive association between mortality and educational level; the higher the educational level, the higher the mortality rate. Reasons for higher education may lower the mortality rate by encouraging patients to seek better means to fight the disease. Our study did not confirm any association between physical activity and the risk of death. Further, education level can also affect a patient’s ability to comply with treatment and participate in early screening. When compared to women who did not get hormonal therapy during the follow-up period, those who took the therapy had a considerably lower mortality rate. Previous studies [ 86 – 88 ] have also shown that hormonal therapy reduced the risk of death among breast cancer patients in the study population. A plausible reason for this might be the effect of hormone therapy on survival improvement was often mentioned along with the influence of hormone receptors. Crowe Jr et al. [ 89 ] concluded that these hormonal receptors contributed to breast cancer patients having higher survival times. Similarly, it was found that women receiving chemotherapy/surgical therapy had a lower likelihood of dying than individuals not receiving chemotherapy/surgical therapy. Despite the strengths of this meta-analysis—including a large pooled sample size, the use of adjusted effect estimates, and broad geographic representation—several limitations should be acknowledged. First, as with all observational meta-analyses, the potential for residual confounding remains. Although we included studies that reported adjusted hazard or odds ratios, the adjustment sets varied across studies, and not all relevant confounders may have been accounted for. Second, there is a possibility of publication bias, as studies reporting non-significant associations or from underrepresented regions may have been less likely to be published or indexed in the databases searched. Although funnel plot symmetry and Egger’s test were not definitive, the risk of bias cannot be entirely excluded. Third, the analysis was based on aggregate data rather than individual patient data (IPD), which limited our ability to perform more granular subgroup analyses and adjust uniformly for confounders. Conclusions In conclusion, this meta-analysis provides comprehensive insights into the diverse clinical, socio-demographic, and lifestyle-related factors that influence breast cancer mortality. The findings underscore the disproportionate burden of mortality in low- and middle-income countries, particularly in Africa, where access to early detection, quality treatment, and follow-up care remains limited. This geographic disparity highlights an urgent need for context-specific policy responses that prioritize health system strengthening, equitable access to cancer care, and targeted prevention strategies in resource-constrained settings. Key modifiable risk factors—such as obesity, smoking, diabetes, and HIV positivity—were consistently associated with increased mortality, reinforcing the importance of integrated non-communicable disease (NCD) prevention within national cancer control programs. Likewise, effective therapeutic interventions—including lumpectomy with radiation, chemotherapy combined with trastuzumab, and hormonal therapy—were associated with significantly improved survival, underscoring the critical need to scale up access to these treatments through universal health coverage, public sector procurement, and workforce capacity building. Furthermore, the elevated mortality observed in patients with Luminal B subtypes, high allostatic load, and advanced age emphasizes the importance of molecular subtyping, psychosocial screening, and early intervention. These findings advocate for personalized care models that incorporate not only biological risk factors but also social determinants of health. For policymakers, these results offer a clear roadmap: invest in cancer registries, subsidize evidence-based treatments, promote early diagnosis through public awareness campaigns, and design targeted interventions for high-risk populations. Addressing both the biomedical and structural drivers of breast cancer mortality is essential to closing the survival gap between high-income countries and LMICs and achieving equity in global cancer outcomes. documents.title: Economic burden of five common cancers in Iran: a systematic review of cost-of-illness with a focus on healthcare resource utilization.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: According to the latest World Health Organization report, approximately half of the new cancer cases in Iran are attributed to five common cancers: gastric, breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer. These cancers impose a heavy economic burden on healthcare systems and society, including direct medical costs (DMC), direct non-medical costs (DNMC), and indirect costs (IDC). This systematic review aimed to investigate the economic burden of these cancers in Iran.
METHODS: This systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. The search strategy was developed using MeSH terms, Emtree, and previous literature. To identify relevant studies published up until December 27, 2023, searches were conducted in both international databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane, and the NHS Economic Evaluation Database) and national databases (SID, Magiran, and IranMedex). After removing duplicates and screening studies using Endnote software, eligible studies were selected for inclusion in the review. The costs were converted to USD 2021 using the CCEMG-EPPI-Centre cost converter.
RESULTS: A total of 22 studies were included in this review. Breast and colorectal cancer each had 4 studies, while prostate, gastric, and lung cancer each had 3 studies. The remaining 5 studies covered a combination of multiple cancers. Converting the costs from different studies to USD 2021 showed that the average annual DMC per patient with breast cancer varied from $13,954 to $34,772. These costs ranged from $14,671 to $28,656 for colorectal cancer, $7,970 to $16,821 for prostate cancer, $12,206 to $17,681 for gastric cancer, and $9,369 to $40,682 for lung cancer. Part of these variations may be related to differences in healthcare resource utilization, while another part may be due to differences in cost calculation methodology, study perspective, and study location. Additional cost conversion findings showed that in 85% of the studies, the average annual DNMC per patient for all cancers were estimated to be less than $4,000. Furthermore, the average annual IDC per patient for breast and lung cancer were estimated to be as high as $100,000 due to high mortality, compared to less than $30,000 for other cancers.
CONCLUSIONS: Given the high prevalence of these five cancers in Iran, their economic burden is significant. Policymakers should focus not only on reducing the disease burden but also on minimizing the economic burden of cancer. Strategies such as improving early detection, optimizing treatment pathways, and implementing cost-effective interventions could help reduce both healthcare costs and the overall financial strain on patients and the healthcare system.
documents.conclusions: Given the high prevalence of these five cancers in Iran, their economic burden is significant. Strategies such as improving early detection, optimizing treatment pathways, and implementing cost-effective interventions could help reduce both healthcare costs and the overall financial strain on patients and the healthcare system.

Background Iran, as a middle-income and developing country, has experienced a growing burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) in recent decades due to demographic and epidemiological transitions, including an aging population and the increase in risk factors such as smoking, poor diet, and physical inactivity [ 1 ]. Among NCDs, cancer is the second leading cause of death and represents a significant portion of the disease burden, imposing a heavy strain on the healthcare system and Iranian society [ 2 ]. According to the latest GLOBOCAN report (published in 2024) on cancer incidence and mortality for the year 2022, more than 137,000 new cancer cases and approximately 87,000 cancer-related deaths occurred in Iran. The report highlights that nearly half of these new cases are attributed to five cancers—stomach (gastric), breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate—which account for the highest incidence rates in the general population (both sexes) [ 3 ]. Furthermore, projections indicate that, after thyroid cancer, prostate, breast, and colorectal cancers will experience the largest increases in new cases by 2025. The total number of new cancer cases is projected to increase by 42.6% compared to 2016, reaching an estimated 160,000 new cases in 2025 [ 4 ]. Additionally, the latest statistics from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021(GBD 2021) highlight that gastric, lung, and breast cancers have the highest disease burden in Iran (measured by Disability-Adjusted Life Years, DALYs), and also, colorectal and prostate cancers rank sixth and eighth, respectively [ 5 ]. Cancer not only affects public health but also significantly impacts the country’s economy [ 6 ]. The increasing economic burden of cancer is a growing concern, particularly as healthcare resources become strained and the demand for cancer treatment rises. Given the high prevalence of these five cancers in Iran, the cost of illness for these cancers is substantial. Cost of illness studies generally classify costs into three categories: direct costs (including direct medical costs (DMC) and direct non-medical costs (DNMC)), indirect costs (IDC), and intangible costs. Since intangible costs are rarely quantified in cost of illness studies due to measurement challenges and related debates, the focus is mainly on the first two categories. DMC refers to the costs of healthcare resource utilization for diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, etc., while DNMC covers non-healthcare resources such as transportation and accommodation. IDC reflects productivity losses due to morbidity and mortality incurred by patients. All these costs contribute to the overall economic burden of disease [ 7 , 8 ]. Therefore, quantification and investigation of these costs for common cancers are necessary to better understand the full impact of the disease. By examining these costs for five cancers, it is possible to determine which factors have the greatest impact on costs and help health managers implement policies with appropriate prioritization. This information can assist policymakers and health planners in making better decisions regarding resource allocation and prioritization. Additionally, examining costs can play an important role in raising awareness among policymakers and health planners about the economic and social burden of cancer. Increased awareness of the financial and economic effects of cancer can help shape positive attitudes and greater attention toward the prevention and management of this disease. Therefore, considering the importance of the issue, this systematic review aimed to investigate the economic burden of five common cancers in Iran: breast, gastric, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer. The qualitative findings of this review can assist researchers in designing future studies on the economic burden of cancer, while the quantitative findings provide valuable data for policymakers to help prevent and reduce the disease burden. Methods This systematic review focuses on five common cancers in Iran: gastric, breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer. These cancer types were selected due to their highest incidence and one-year prevalence rates for the general population (both sexes), as reported in the latest GLOBOCAN 2022 data. The selection reflects the significant public health impact and economic burden these cancers pose to the Iranian society. Detailed incidence and prevalence rates are provided in the Supplementary Material 1 . This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 9 ]. The completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided in the Supplementary Material 2 . Review question What is the economic burden of five common cancers in Iran? Eligibility criteria All the studies that investigated the cost of illness or the economic burden of five common cancers in Iran were reviewed without considering the time limit. The exclusion criteria for the review include the following: (1) Types of studies such as editorials, letters to the editor, systematic and non-systematic review, meta-analysis, case reports, clinical trials, and conference summaries. (2) Studies that estimated case-specific components of cancer costs (e.g., only surgery or drugs, etc.). (3) Studies that have dealt with only specific analyses such as cost-effectiveness, cost-utility, cost-benefit, and cost minimization. Determining data sources Scientific sources included original studies available in international databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane, and the NHS Economic Evaluation Database. In this review, manual searches in Google and Google Scholar were also used to complete the review and make it comprehensive. In addition, gray literature was reviewed using a modified search strategy from the OpenGrey database. The Scientific Information Database (SID), Magiran, and IranMedex national databases were also used to search for studies published in Persian. The search was conducted in these databases without any time limitations, covering all studies published up until December 27, 2023. Search strategy design The search strategy was designed using PEO components. In this review, the population (P) considered for the search of published studies included any individual or groups of Iranian nationality, regardless of age, gender, race, or socioeconomic status, who were exposed (E) to the five common cancers. The outcome (O) sought information on healthcare resource utilization and the economic burden associated with exposure to these five cancers. The keywords related to these components were identified from Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, Emtree, and previous literature. To consider language and terminology differences, national databases (SID, Magiran, and IranMedex) were searched using equivalent Persian terms for selected keywords. After identifying the appropriate keywords, search strategies were developed for each database by balancing sensitivity and accuracy indicators. The developed strategy for searching in four international databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase) is provided in Supplementary Material 3 . Selection of relevant studies At this step of the review, studies were extracted from selected databases according to the developed search strategy. Duplicates were then removed using Endnote V.20.2.1 software. The remaining studies underwent screening based on the eligibility criteria in two phases. The first phase involved screening based on the title and abstract, while the second phase involved screening based on the full text. The screening process was performed by two reviewers (KI and JA) independently, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus with a third reviewer (VA). The screening of studies followed PRISMA principles. Data collection and extraction A tool was created using Excel 2016 software to collect data required for the variables of this review from the studies. The tool included three tables: one for the characteristics of the included studies, one for cost components of the included studies and one for cost findings of the included studies. The table of study characteristics included variables such as the study’s target population, perspective, time frame, sample size, sampling method, currency, costing year, discount rate, and study design method. The table of cost components included the cost items, their data sources, and their cost calculation methods for three cost groups: direct medical costs (DMC), direct non-medical costs (DNMC), and indirect costs (IDC). The table of cost findings included the cost results and cost synthesis for these three cost groups. Data synthesis In this review, cost findings were converted to 2021 United States dollar (USD) using the Campbell and Cochrane Economics Methods Group Evidence for Policy and Practice Information and Coordination Centre (CCEMG-EPPI-Centre) cost converter (v.1.7, last updated: January 2024). In this converter, we used the International Monetary Fund (IMF) method, which adjusts costs based on purchasing power parity (PPP) values. The IMF method first adjusts costs using the Gross Domestic Product Deflator index, which accounts for inflation and economic conditions in each country. Then, the adjusted costs are converted to USD using PPP exchange rates, which account for differences in purchasing power between countries [ 10 ]. The year 2021 was selected for conversion because among the studies included in this review, the most recent year of cost calculation was 2021. Quality assessment of studies In this review, quality assessment was performed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ 11 ]. This scale has recently been applied to assess quality in several reviews on the economic burden of cancer [ 12 – 14 ]. The NOS is a multi-star system, originally designed for cohort and case-control studies, but modified versions are available for evaluating the quality of cross-sectional studies. The modified NOS assesses the methodological rigor of cross-sectional studies, similarly to cohort studies, across three domains: selection, comparability, and outcome, which are also applicable to retrospective studies. The population selection domain evaluated sample representativeness (4 or 5 stars), the population comparability domain evaluated the comparability of subjects (2 stars), and the outcome domain evaluated statistical testing and outcome assessment (3 stars) [ 12 ]. A quality score for each study was calculated by summing the awarded stars. Thus, studies with ≥ 8 stars were categorized as high-quality, 5–7 stars as moderate quality, and ≤ 4 stars as low quality [ 15 ]. Results Overview A total of 6,179 studies were retrieved by searching the developed search strategy in the databases. After removing duplicate studies using Endnote V.20.2.1 software, 4,593 studies entered the screening phase. During the first phase of screening, studies were reviewed based on the title and abstract. In this phase, 4,533 studies were excluded due to irrelevance, leaving 60 studies for the second phase of screening. In the second phase, the full text of the remaining studies was examined, resulting in the exclusion of 37 studies due to a lack of eligibility criteria. Among these, 2 studies were excluded despite meeting the criteria due to incorrect outcomes [ 16 , 17 ]. Finally, a quality assessment was conducted for the remaining 23 studies. One article was excluded due to low quality [ 18 ]. Among the assessed studies, 22 received acceptable grades (6 with good quality and 16 with moderate quality) and remained for the final review (Fig. 1 ). The quality assessment results are provided in the Supplementary Material 4 . Fig. 1 PRISMA diagram of the search and selection process Characteristics of included studies Among the 22 studies included in this review, 4 studies related to breast cancer [ 19 – 22 ], 4 studies related to colorectal cancer [ 23 – 26 ], 3 studies related to prostate cancer [ 27 – 29 ], 3 studies related to gastric cancer [ 30 – 32 ], 3 studies related to lung cancer [ 33 – 35 ], and 5 studies related to a combination of multiple cancers [ 36 – 40 ]. Most of these studies examined costs from a societal perspective ( N = 7) and patient’s perspective ( N = 7). The time period for most studies was 1 year ( N = 9). Among the studies that mentioned the sampling method in their report, the census method ( N = 6) followed by the random sampling method ( N = 4) had the largest number. The sample size in most studies was below 200 people ( N = 8). In most studies, the costs were reported in USD ( N = 18). The study design method in most studies was cross-sectional ( N = 14) (Table 1 , Fig. 2 ). The costs of diagnostic services include the costs of initial tests, chemotherapy tests, follow-up tests, mammography, and other diagnostic laboratory and radiology services. Colorectal cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for colorectal cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, inpatient hospital care (such as the costs of inpatient drugs, nursing care, and use of inpatient resources), diagnostic services, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, rehabilitation such as physiotherapy, as well as medication and drugs. The costs of diagnostic services include laboratory tests, pathology, computed tomography scan (CT scan), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasonography, electrocardiography, electroencephalography, radiography, nuclear medicine, endoscopy, and other diagnostic laboratory and radiology services [ 23 – 26 ] (Table 2 ). In Jafari et al.’s study, the average DMC per colorectal cancer patient in 2019 were estimated to be $4,301 (1 USD = 42,000 IRR) [ 23 ]. In Nejati et al.’s study, these costs for 2016 were equivalent to $17,038 (1 USD = 8,212.15 IRR) [ 24 ], and in Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study for 2012 and in Davari et al.’s study for 2011, the costs were equivalent to $4,242 (1 USD = 12,229 IRR) and $7,768 (1 USD = 10,965 IRR), respectively [ 25 , 26 ]. Additionally, Jafari et al. estimated the total costs for colorectal cancer in 2019 to be $46 million for the whole country. In the study by Vahdatimanesh et al. in 2012, these total costs were estimated at $96 million (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with colorectal cancer in different studies varied from $14,671 to $28,656 (mean = $20,840; median = $20,016) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per colorectal cancer patient in Jafari et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of accommodation, transportation of patients and companions, food for the patient and companions, special diet, changing the home environment to adapt to the disease, telephone and internet calls to family, babysitters and kindergartens, and purchase of aids, were estimated at $949 in 2019 [ 23 ]. These costs were estimated to be $4,388 in 2016 in the study by Nejati et al., who included the costs of guardian services and hoteling as DNMC [ 24 ]. In Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study in 2012, the costs were approximately $1,297, considering the costs of patient time and transportation as DNMC [ 25 ]. Jafari et al. estimated these costs for the whole country to be $10 million, while Vahdatimanesh et al. estimated them at $29 million (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per colorectal cancer patient in these studies varied from $3,526 to $6,193 (mean = $4,735; median= $4,485) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per colorectal cancer patient in the study by Jafari et al. in 2019 were estimated to be $495 [ 23 ]. In Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study, these costs were estimated to be approximately $7,659 per patient and $173 million for the whole country in 2012 [ 25 ]. In Jafari et al.’s study, these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, whereas in Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study, these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per colorectal cancer patient in these two studies were $1,841 and $26,490, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Prostate cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for prostate cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services (such as imaging and cystoscopy, laboratory and pathology services), surgery (including radical prostatectomy and orchiectomy surgery), radiotherapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, rehabilitation, as well as medication and drugs (such as antiandrogens and luteinizing hormone agonists) [ 27 – 29 ] (Table 2 ). In Alinezhad et al.’s study, the average DMC per prostate cancer patient in 2018 were estimated to be $3,773 PPP (exchange rate not reported) [ 27 ]. In Foroughi Moghadam et al.’s study, these costs for 2015 were equivalent to $2,934 (1 USD = 29,580 IRR) [ 28 ]. Mojahidian et al.’s study in 2016 reported these costs by different disease states, ranging from $103 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $7,748 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer (exchange rate not reported) [ 29 ]. The DMC of prostate cancer for the whole country were estimated at $2 million in Alinezhad et al.’s study and $12.5 million in Foroughi Moghadam et al.’s study (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with prostate cancer in different studies varied from $7,970 to $16,821 (mean = $13,704; median = $16,320) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per prostate cancer patient in Alinezhad et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of transportation, accommodation, and a disease-specific diet in 2018, were estimated to be $186 PPP [ 27 ]. In the study by Mojahidian et al., these costs, considering the costs of intra-city and inter-city travel to receive services, hotel accommodation, and food consumed during the trip in 2016, varied from $97 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $1,068 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer [ 29 ]. In the study by Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs were estimated to be approximately $200 per patient and $898 thousand for the whole country based on the new cases identified in 2015, considering the costs of transportation and accommodation as DNMC [ 28 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per prostate cancer patient in these studies varied from $300 to $2,652 (mean = $1,374; median = $1,171) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per prostate cancer patient in the study by Alinezhad et al. in 2018 were estimated to be $1,307 PPP [ 27 ]. These costs varied based on different disease states and were reported in the study by Mojahidian et al. in 2016, ranging from $24 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $358 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer [ 29 ]. In the study by Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs were estimated to be approximately $2,920 per patient and $12 million for the whole country, based on the new cases identified in 2015 [ 28 ]. Alinezhad et al. included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death. However, in the studies by Mojahidian et al. and Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and the patient’s family (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per prostate cancer patient in these three studies were $10,857, $739, and $16,239, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Gastric cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for gastric cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services (such as initial tests, pre-chemotherapy tests, follow-up tests, CT scan, MRI, ultrasonography, endoscopy, colonoscopy, and other diagnostic laboratory and radiology services), surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, as well as medication and drugs (including the costs of chemotherapy drugs, supportive drugs) [ 30 – 32 ] (Table 2 ). In the study by Jalilian et al., the average DMC per gastric cancer patient in 2017 were estimated to be $3,288 (1 USD = 32,441 IRR) [ 30 ]. In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs for 2016 were equivalent to $2,350 (1 USD = 30,221 IRR) [ 31 ]. In the study by Izadi et al., these costs in 2015 were estimated to be 113,370,129 Rials for the private sector and 74,705,158 Rials for the public sector [ 32 ] (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with gastric cancer in different studies varied from $12,206 to $17,681 (mean = $15,369; median = $16,220) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per gastric cancer patient in Jalilian et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of travel, accommodation, and food in 2017, were estimated to be $378 [ 30 ]. In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs were equal to $522 for 2016, considering the costs of transportation, accommodation, food for the patient and relatives, the patient’s consumables, and the accommodation of the people who visit the patient at his, her home [ 31 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per gastric cancer patient in these studies varied from $1,862 to $2,711 (mean = median = $2,287) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per gastric cancer patient in the study by Jalilian et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $505 [ 30 ]. I In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs for 2016 were equal to $1,094 [ 31 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and the patient’s companions (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per gastric cancer patient in these two studies were $2,493 and $5,682, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Lung cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for lung cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, physiotherapy, as well as medication and drugs [ 33 – 35 ] (Table 2 ). In Mir et al.’s study, the average DMC per lung cancer patient in 2016 were estimated to be $7,542 (exchange rate not reported) [ 33 ]. In Mohagheghi et al.’s study, these costs for 2009 were equivalent to $1,932 (1 USD = 9,917 IRR) [ 35 ]. Additionally, Mohagheghi et al. estimated the total costs for lung cancer in 2009 to be $11 million for the whole country based on the incidence of the disease. In Rezaei et al.’s study, these total costs were estimated to be 350 billion Rials for the whole country based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ] (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with lung cancer in different studies varied from $9,369 to $40,682 (mean = $21,280; median = $13,785) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). In the study by Mir et al., the average DNMC per lung cancer patient in 2016, taking into account the costs of transportation, food, and accommodation, were estimated to be $499 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs, considering transportation, accommodation, food, care for family members such as the elderly or children, and other service costs such as telephone bills for the whole country based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014, were estimated at 87 billion Rials [ 34 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per lung cancer patient in these studies varied from $2,690 to $3,428 (mean = median = $3,059) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per lung cancer patient in the study by Mir et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $11,903 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs for the whole country were estimated to be approximately 584 million Rials per patient and 2,789 billion Rials based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per lung cancer patient in these two studies were $64,207 and $110,015, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per lung cancer patient in the study by Mir et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $11,903 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs for the whole country were estimated to be approximately 584 million Rials per patient and 2,789 billion Rials based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per lung cancer patient in these two studies were $64,207 and $110,015, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Discussion As the findings indicate, the healthcare resource utilization or cost items for DMC may vary depending on the type of cancer, while the cost items for DNMC and IDC are similar for all cancers. Most of the differences among cost items for DMC are linked to diagnostic services. For instance, one of the cost items for breast cancer that other cancers do not have is the diagnostic cost of mammography. Similarly, one of the cost items for colorectal cancer that other cancers do not have is the diagnostic cost of colonoscopy. This highlights the importance of recognizing the unique cost drivers for each cancer type in healthcare planning, as they contribute significantly to the overall economic burden. Converting the costs from different studies to USD 2021 showed that the average annual DMC per patient with breast cancer in Iran varied from $13,954 to $34,772 [ 19 – 22 ]. These costs range from $14,671 to $28,656 for colorectal cancer [ 23 – 26 ], $7,970 to $16,821 for prostate cancer [ 27 – 29 ], $12,206 to $17,681 for gastric cancer [ 30 – 32 ], and $9,369 to $40,682 for lung cancer [ 33 – 35 ]. Part of this variation is related to the different healthcare resource utilization or cost items considered for cost calculation. Another part may be due to differences in cost calculation methodology, study perspective, and study location (private or public sector). The observed cost variation reflects the complex interplay of healthcare policies, resource availability, and methodological choices across different studies. Since these five cancers are the most common cancers in Iran, multiplying these costs by the total number of people with cancer makes the total cost for the country significant. For example, in the study by Daroudi et al. in 2010, the costs for breast cancer in the whole country were estimated at $176 million [ 21 ]. Therefore, the researchers emphasize that the disease burden is one dimension of the problem, and the other dimension is the economic burden of the disease, which, if not addressed, can have significant effects on the country’s health economics. Without targeted policies to reduce diagnostic and treatment costs, this economic pressure may challenge the sustainability of Iran’s healthcare system. The cost items for DNMC are similar across all cancers. These items include the costs of accommodation, transportation for patients and companions (both intra-city and inter-city), food for patients and companions, special diets, telephone and internet communication with family, purchasing auxiliary equipment, patient consumables, modifying the home environment to adapt to the disease, childcare, eldercare, kindergarten services, hiring a housemaid, and accommodating visitors at the patient’s home [ 19 – 21 , 23 – 25 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. However, due to limitations in measuring these costs, some cost items might be ignored or simpler methods might be used to measure them. Ignoring certain DNMC items may lead to an underestimation of the total economic burden, especially in cases where these costs are substantial, potentially resulting in insufficient resource allocation and inadequate support for patients and their families. Based on USD 2021, in 85% of studies (11 out of 13 studies), the average annual DNMC per patient are estimated to be less than $4,000 for each patient suffering from one of these five cancers [ 19 – 21 , 23 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. In other studies, (2 out of 13 studies), these costs were more than $4,000 that were related to colorectal cancer [ 24 , 25 ]. This finding suggests that DNMC, though generally lower than DMC, still represent a significant burden, particularly for cancers like colorectal cancer where these costs exceed $4,000, underscoring the need for comprehensive support systems for cancer patients and their families. The authors believe that the similarity in DNMC across cancers reflects broader socioeconomic impacts on patients and their families, highlighting the need for universal support services that address non-medical costs among cancer patients. IDC, like DNMC, have similar cost items across all cancers. These items include the costs of lost productivity due to the patient’s absence from work, the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient’s companions who care for them, and the costs of lost productivity due to premature death [ 19 – 21 , 23 – 25 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. It is important to consider that due to limitations in measurement, some of these cost items may be ignored in studies, or they may be measured based on assumptions. Since the death and disability rate is much higher in some cancers compared to others, the variance of these costs may be significant among different cancers. For instance, based on USD 2021, the average annual IDC per patient with breast and lung cancer, due to high mortality, were approximately $100,000 [ 34 ], while for other cancers, the average annual IDC were less than $30,000 [ 25 , 27 ]. The researchers conclude that the high IDC associated with cancers like breast and lung cancer, driven by high mortality rates, calls for more preventive and early detection programs to reduce productivity loss. Focusing on these high-mortality cancers could further help alleviate both individual and national economic burdens. Given the complexity of measuring, future research could focus on refining cost measurement techniques, particularly for DNMC and IDC, and addressing methodological differences across studies. Additionally, exploring how integrating cancer support services, such as palliative care, psychological support, and family care, might reduce some of these non-medical and indirect costs would be valuable. Limitations Since this review is related to Iran and almost all studies from this country have been published in Persian and English, we did not face significant language limitations. However, since most of the studies focus on specific regions or healthcare settings within Iran, the findings may not be fully generalizable to all regions or healthcare environments in the country. Additionally, due to the nature of the search strategy and the selected databases, there is always the possibility of missing studies in a systematic review. To reduce this limitation, we developed a detailed search strategy and selected diverse databases. Finally, due to the heterogeneous nature of cost definitions and measurements among the included studies in this review, comparing costs across studies was difficult. Therefore, in the study findings section, efforts were made to compare costs more cautiously, and for this purpose, the findings have been reported in more detail. Conclusion Cancer encompasses a wide range of resources and cost items. For researchers to accurately examine DMC, DNMC, and IDC in future studies, they should aim to include all or at least most of these cost items in their calculations. Despite the limitations in calculating some of these costs, findings from studies indicate that the costs associated with the five most common cancers in Iran are significant. Therefore, efforts by policymakers to combat cancer should not only focus on reducing the burden of the disease but also aim to alleviate the economic burden it imposes. To achieve this, policymakers could consider implementing more efficient resource allocation strategies, enhancing access to early detection and preventive programs, and investing in cost-effective treatment protocols. Additionally, establishing financial support systems for patients, particularly for non-medical costs, could mitigate the economic challenges faced by cancer patients and their families. documents.title: Diagnostic accuracy of ESR1 mutation detection by cell-free DNA in breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Estrogen receptors express in nearly 70% of breast cancers (ER-positive). Estrogen receptor alpha plays a fundamental role as a significant factor in breast cancer progression for the early selection of therapeutic approaches. Accordingly, there has been a surge of attention to non-invasive techniques, including circulating Cell-free DNA (ccfDNA) or Cell-Free DNA (cfDNA), to detect and track ESR1 genotype. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the diagnosis accuracy of ESR1 mutation detection by cell-free DNA in breast cancer patientsthrough a systematic review and comprehensive meta-analysis.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science databases were searched up to 6 April 2022. Diagnostic studies on ESR1 measurement by cfDNA, which was confirmed using the tumour tissue biopsy, have been included in the study. The sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) were considered to analyse the data.
RESULTS: Out of 649 papers, 13 papers with 15 cohorts, including 389 participants, entered the meta-analyses. The comprehensive meta-analysis indicated a high sensitivity (75.52, 95% CI 60.19-90.85), specificity (88.20, 95% CI 80.99-95.40), and high accuracy of 88.96 (95% CI 83.23-94.69) for plasma ESR1. We also found a moderate PPV of 56.94 (95% CI 41.70-72.18) but a high NPV of 88.53 (95% CI 82.61-94.44). We also found an NLR of 0.443 (95% CI 0.09-0.79) and PLR of 1.60 (95% CI 1.20-1.99).
CONCLUSION: This systematic review and comprehensive meta-analysis reveal that plasma cfDNA testing exhibits high sensitivity and specificity in detecting ESR1 mutations in breast cancer patients. This suggests that the test could be a valuable diagnostic tool. It may serve as a dependable and non-invasive technique for identifying ESR1 mutations in breast cancer patients. However, more extensive research is needed to confirm its prognostic value.
documents.conclusions: This systematic review and comprehensive meta-analysis reveal that plasma cfDNA testing exhibits high sensitivity and specificity in detecting ESR1 mutations in breast cancer patients. This suggests that the test could be a valuable diagnostic tool. It may serve as a dependable and non-invasive technique for identifying ESR1 mutations in breast cancer patients. However, more extensive research is needed to confirm its prognostic value.
